paragraphs.text: It is a manifestation of the work of God in a believer that he would desire to be always in the path of the will of God, and to be in the path of the will of God involves dependence on God. There is a great need for dependence on God. The tendency is to fall back upon our own resources and our own strength to resolve the issues as to the path in which we should walk.

We tend to fall back perhaps on our own powers of analysis, and the determination of our own wills, but the, path of a believer is essentially a path of dependence. I would encourage the brethren to be more dependent, to cry to God continually in regard to their pathway through this world. These scriptures bring up the thought of the pathway of the believer through this scene, so that, we do not tread it with an uncertain step. To me it would be a reflection on the indwelling of the Spirit, if we reconciled ourselves to the thought that there must always be uncertainty as to our movements, and as to who could be certain as to the path in which a believer should walk in these days. It is a reflection on the Spirit to allow such thoughts, and these Scriptures bring out the wonderful sources of divine help and divine direction which give the believer certainty in his path.

There was a little publication which was a help to many of us in our younger days—it is still available I am sure in the bookcases of the elder brethren—by a beloved brother. Mr. M. W. Biggs, it is ‘The Christian’s Path in Days of Difficulty’. He pointed out that, no matter what the morass of evil that exists in this world, it is possible for a christian to find his true path despite the difficulty of the day; but linked with it there must undoubtedly be this feature of constant dependence. What comes out in the typical scriptures, and actually in the gospels as to the dependence of our Lord Jesus Christ as a Man here, is something that always enthralls the heart. The Lord Jesus was God. He was God as to His Person, but what comes out in the Scriptures indicates that He never called upon what He was in Deity to govern Him in His pathway here. It is a remarkable thing. The natural mind would say, Well, if He was God how could He not resolve for Himself any matter? And yet He went up in the mountain to be tempted by the devil, and many other instances I could quote, and what comes to light is His absolute dependence.

Younger brethren, you go to school and college, you take up your employment, and you know there are difficulties to be faced. I would encourage you to be dependent; be dependent even in regard to what you might say if you are faced with a certain situation; when men would dispute your right to a conscience in regard to the claims of God, be dependent as to what the Lord might give you to say at any such time.

So you have to think of the Lord Jesus; it says, “I have set Jehovah continually before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. Therefore my heart rejoiceth, and my glory exulteth; my flesh moreover shall dwell in hope. For thou wilt not leave my soul to Sheol, neither wilt thou allow thy Holy One to see corruption. Thou wilt make known to me the path of life”. You ponder that statement, it is as if the Lord Jesus was receiving disclosures from His Father as to the pathway that would be in life, “Thou wilt make known to me the path of life”. Dear brethren, have you ever asked the Father for a disclosure to you of the path of life? You could say, Well, I know there is a certain pathway through this world which would lead me to material prosperity. Another pathway would lead to prominence in this world. Another pathway would lead to the satisfaction of my natural affections, my natural desires. But have you ever had a disclosure from the Father as to the path of life? The Lord Jesus as a Man here had that experience. We speak very, very reverently, but it was just as if the Lord clung in absolute, holy dependence on God so that He would not be diverted in any sense from the pathway of His will.

O, young brethren, find the path of life! Whatever you do, find the path of life; find that which nurtures your soul, nurtures your spirit, nurtures your affections in the things of God, so that the Scriptures become something to you, and as you read them your heart expands as you trace the features of Jesus. The path of life involves, too, what we said earlier as to the fellowship amongst God’s people. In this world today it is a path of death, but amongst God’s people it is a path of life. The assembly is a sphere of salvation, and of protection, and you will find in that path God’s “countenance is fulness of joy; at thy right hand are pleasures for evermore”. The path of life leads you to then “pleasures for evermore”. I find nothing so stimulating as we gather for the Lord’s supper on the first day of the week as to touch the pleasures for evermore, to know that the path of life has led to the place where the divine countenance beams in all its brightness, “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4: 6), to taste the pleasures that belong to eternity, and to feel our souls surging up in holy power and emotion as the living Head leads us into that vast realm of bliss where God shows His treasures, His wonderful thoughts and purpose. How many pathways beckon today. The Lord says, “broad the way that leads to destruction, and many are they who enter in through it”, but straitened is the way that leads to life, and they are few who find it (Matthew 7: 13, 14). But it is the path of life, and I trust we will be encouraged in it.

Now in Psalm 119 I wish to speak of “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path”. I would like to emphasize, beloved brethren, the importance of the Holy Scriptures in the life of a believer if he is to walk in a right path. How do we value the Scriptures? How do we read them? It is quite a challenge to me personally as moving about amongst God’s people, how I tend to use the Scriptures to provide me with themes for ministry, instead of valuing the Scriptures as a lamp for my feet and a light unto my path. You know why you need a lamp and a light, do you not? When you go out on a dark night and you do not know if there is going to be something you will stumble over, you say, I will take a light. You know, this world is full of things you can stumble over. Jude says, “to him that is able to keep you without stumbling” (Jude 24). You do not want to stumble, dear brethren. When David took up the ark, it says that the oxen stumbled (2 Samuel 6: 6). God would have a believer that has the Spirit walk without stumbling. And how do you walk without stumbling? It says, “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet”.

Oh, the precious Scriptures!—and the precious ministry that is based on Scripture, giving its current application according to our needs; it is a lamp unto our feet. A matter comes up and you say, What am I going to do in that pathway? Where am I going to go in that pathway? You turn to the Scriptures. The Scriptures are an unfailing guide for any person as to the right pathway. You want to go into business? You say, ‘I want a lamp for my feet’; the Scriptures will guide you. You want to marry? you want to set up a home? The Scripture will guide you. You want to know who to walk with in Christian fellowship? The Scripture will guide you. There is not a thing that comes within the area of a believer’s responsibility but what the Scripture will give him guidance by the help of the Holy Spirit.

Much of the sorrow that has come in amongst brethren lies in the misinterpretation and the misapplication of Scripture. We should value the purity of it, value the fact that by the Spirit it is the expression of the mind of God to us in detail. It says, “a light unto my path”. Oh, to go through this world with a light for your path! Just to know what to side-step, and where to move and where to go, because you have the light of the Holy Scriptures. I would counsel my young brethren to read the ministry, but above all else read the Scriptures, and turn to them continually for guidance in regard to your pathway.

Also seek the help of the fathers, seek the help of your own father. There is nothing so delightful as a boy or a girl going to their father and saying to him, ‘Father, you are the head of the house, I would like you to direct me to a scripture that will help me in this matter that affects my pathway’. Noah put a light at the top of the ark, in other words, typically, he brought in for his household the scripture that met the exigencies of the moment.

In Jeremiah 6 we read, “Thus saith Jehovah—Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls”. As the brethren will know, Jeremiah writes in a day very similar to the day in which we live; there had been a complete breakdown among God’s people, conditions were very oppressive, he had been subjected to very much sorrow, and the people had departed and come under the yoke of the enemy. And he says here, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the ancient paths”. Now, beloved brethren, I think there is a need today to ask for the ancient paths. The ancient paths, of course, would refer primarily to the apostles’ doctrine, the ministries of the apostles and the prophets. It would also refer to what has come out since the inception of the recovery. Now I would like to ask a question, which I have asked a few times lately: Is everybody amongst us here at this time convicted that there was, and is, such a thing as the recovery of the truth? Are we all convicted that what took place early in the nineteenth century was a recovery of the truth initiated by the Spirit of God and directed from heaven by the Lord Himself? Are we all convicted about that?

I do not want to be critical, but I cannot see for myself how a person who was convicted that there was such a thing as the recovery of the truth under Mr. Darby and others could possibly go back to a clerical system. In the recovery of the truth under Mr. Darby, the signpost to the ancient path is set forth in his pamphlet, ‘The Notion of a Clergyman, Dispensationally the Sin Against the Holy Ghost’. And so, let us ask for the ancient paths. Let us see what has been wrought out in the recovery as to the truth of the assembly, the truth of what is for the pleasure of God, the great matters of the fellowship and the service of God. Let us seek the ancient paths, and walk in them, too; it says, “which is the good way, and walk therein”. The elder brethren in localities, fathers, have a great responsibility to teach younger brethren, to teach from the Scriptures and from the ministries the ancient paths, so that they walk in them. It is a good way; it says, “and ye shall find rest for your souls”. That is a beautiful touch. The Lord said in Matthew 11: 28, 29, “Come to me, all ye who labour and are burdened ... Take my yoke upon you ... and ye shall find rest to your souls”, and here it is in Jeremiah. In Matthew 11 the Lord gave utterance to these words in the face of His rejection by God’s earthly people. You look round, and you think of brethren you once walked with and your heart goes out to them. You love the brethren; though you cannot walk with them, you love them; and you find rest in your soul in turning to the Lord.

As long as you are doing the will of God and keeping steadfastly to the ancient paths the Spirit of God has marked out, you will find it is a good way in which to walk, and indeed leads to the path of life.

In Hebrews 12: 12–14 it says, “Wherefore lift up the hands that hang down, and the failing knees”; that would be a reference to prayer. Do your knees ever fail? Do your knees ever fail when you become weary of prayer because there is no answer? Well, it says, lift up the hands that hang down, and the failing knees; and make straight paths for your feet. There is the path of life; there is the path that is illuminated by the Scriptures; there are the ancient paths; but here is the straight path, a straight path for your feet. It says, “that that which is lame be not turned aside”. It is the responsibility of the shepherds in a place to look out for the lame sheep, so that they are not turned out of the way, “but that rather it may be healed”. Luke’s gospel is a great healing gospel, the grace that comes in to heal. Luke brings out; too, the sheep that went astray in chapter 15; it had gone out of the path, and the Lord speaks of Himself there as the Shepherd that went after the sheep in order to bring it back into the right path.

So it says, “make straight paths for your feet, that that which is lame be not turned aside; but that rather it may be healed. Pursue peace with all”. Brethren, there is no virtue in contention. A bondman of the Lord should not contend (see 2 Timothy 2: 24). You may say, Am I not to contend for the truth? Yes, you are to contend for the truth. A bondman of the Lord, a good soldier of Jesus Christ, contends for the truth. But it also says he “should not contend”. O, brethren, let us pursue peace with all, and not regard contention as a virtue. The need universally in our localities at the present time is peace, in order that conditions may exist for the building up of the saints in the truth and the restoration to the ancient pathways. Matters of righteousness come up that have got to be contended for, matters of fellowship, matters of principle, they have got to be contended for by faithful men. But, brethren, let us make peace our objective so that the Lord gets full scope to bring in what is for the blessing of His people.

The scripture then says, “and holiness”. In the reading a brother referred to what is objective. The note in Mr. Darby’s translation directs us to the fact that the word “holiness” here is not a sanctification outwardly but it stands in relation to a state. Holiness flows from the recognition of the Spirit’s witness to the water and the blood. A saint who recognised the Spirit’s witness to the water and the blood would be formed subjectively in holiness. The scripture adds “without which no one shall see the Lord”. Beloved brethren, we are looking forward to seeing the Lord tomorrow, if it is His will, if He tarry. What would a meeting be if we did not see the Lord? What would the Supper be if we did not see the Lord? That is why you leave your house in the morning; you leave your house in the expectation of seeing the Lord; but how do you see Him? With holiness, so that we are preserved here in purity of thought and purity of walk that provide the conditions for the Lord to come to us. May we encourage one another, old and young alike, to walk in the path of the will of God for His pleasure.

articles.title: THE LORD’S PERSONAL SERVICE
articles.author: E. M. Walkinshaw
articles.meeting: Word at the burial of Mr, A. J. Ellis

paragraphs.text: The personal service of Jesus has already been twice referred to, dear brethren, that He has put our brother to sleep. I would like to speak of the affection that enters into that, and to say that Jesus could have said of our brother “our friend”. Mr. Percy Lyon once said that Jesus does not say of Lazarus ‘our late friend’ but “our friend”. Yet Jesus waits two days then He says, “I go that I may awake him out of sleep”. I think it is very touching that Jesus should give personal attention to each believer who falls asleep before the rapture, and He has given personal attention to our brother. It has often been said that the burial of a saint is not the time to eulogize the dead but the living, and therefore if there is a eulogy in this occasion it must be of the living, and that is of Jesus. I am sure if it were possible—which it is not that our brother could hear what I have just said, he would say ‘Amen’, as indeed we all would. But Jesus says, “I go that I may awake him out of sleep”. What it meant to Jesus that “Lazarus, our friend, is fallen asleep”. Of course, He says plainly later that he is dead, but in the glory of the power of the Son of God He is able to raise him from the dead, and if He can raise one person from the dead He can raise myriads from the dead, as it has so often been said. Hence I thought of speaking of the affection of Jesus that enters into putting a saint to sleep.

Our brother has had that experience, which we have not, and we rejoice that our brother is now with Christ, which is very much better. But when Jesus says, “I go that I may awake him out of sleep”. He is suggesting that He is on the way. Two days He waited, and in the way in which He speaks to the angel of the assembly in Philadelphia it is as though He is on the way.

He does not say, ‘I will come quickly’, but “I come quickly”, suggesting that He is on the way to awaken every believer out of sleep and to catch up together with them every living believer to be for ever with Himself; none will be overlooked. Jesus has been on the way, in His affections, if I may say it without being fanciful, for nearly two thousand years. I do not wish to make too much of the two days and the two thousand years, although one day in the sight of the Lord is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day. There may be something in it, because in Scripture there are hidden depths which we have not yet fathomed, if we ever will, but the point I desire to make is as to the love of Christ; He died for us. He died for our sins, and He was buried, and He was raised again the third day according to the Scriptures, and I think I can say, beloved brethren, He is on the way when He says, “I come quickly”.

Then He adds, “hold fast what thou hast”; the words given in this meeting are not for our brother, they are for us. Our brother has given us an example; the Lord would give us a word so that we might hold fast what we have, and that we might fill the ranks so that the testimony of our Lord might be carried through until it finds its consummation in glory.

May we all be comforted, dear brethren, especially our sister. She will know a touch from the Lord which we shall not know in quite the same way; we ask Him to grant it to her. He will, whether we ask or not, but we are glad to ask Him to grant it to her and to any other sorrowing relatives too. But let us remember that in His heart the Lord is carrying every saint and He is on the way to catch them all up to be with Himself. May our hearts be very much encouraged by it for His name’s sake.

A study of these opening chapters of Chronicles is rewarding spiritually. One thing we can trace in them is the vital, unbroken line of the testimony. There are many names mentioned and here and there the Holy Spirit makes comments as to certain persons who are worthy of our consideration for they are full of spiritual meaning, as, for instance, what He says as to Jabez and others in chapter 4, and as to Judah and Joseph in chapter 5. Each comment provides much food for thought. In this section He is going over the sons of Kohath, and He mentions the names of a number of persons well known in the history of the testimony, but when He comes to Azariah He makes this most interesting comment, “He is it that exercised the priesthood in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem”. Here is a man exercising the most dignified service in the most dignified surroundings possible and the Spirit says of him, “He is it”. He would arrest our attention by this statement and cause us to consider what it means. He could have said simply, ‘He exercised the priesthood’, but He says designedly, “He is it”, for He would impress upon us what the man is in reality, what he is substantially, morally, and spiritually.

The burden of the reading today was reality in view of the Supper and the service of God, and we see this feature set out in Azariah. Morally and spiritually he was equal to the great service he was fulfilling in the glorious circumstances in which he was fulfilling it. He was it, the real thing. In this matter, of course, as in all else, our thoughts would turn to the Lord Jesus for in all things He must have the first place; in all things He must be the Standard and Model. In John 8, that great chapter of conflict, His opposers question Him, “Who art thou?”—He answered, “Altogether that which I also say to you”. The footnote there reads, ‘His speech presented Himself, being the truth’. The Lord Jesus was what He said He was, and He was what He was wherever He was. It was morally impossible for Him to be anything else than what He was. We can understand then that this feature of reality is very attractive to Him. He appreciates it and He is looking for it amongst us. As we read the gospels we can see how reality appealed to His affections, as, for example, the woman of Luke 7. He called the attention of Simon, that pretentious Pharisee, to that woman who was the real thing. He virtually says, ‘She is it’. If we appear to be the real thing when amongst the brethren and are something else when not amongst them, that is just hypocrisy. The strong language that the Lord uses as to hypocrisy shows what He thinks about it, and His judgment must be ours. If there is any element of hypocrisy with any of us, let us judge it unsparingly in the light of the Lord’s judgment of it and in the light of what it cost Him to deal with it, those untold sufferings on the cross.

We can see right down through the history of the testimony how the Lord Jesus is attracted to what is real. In these days when we are surrounded by what is depicted in Thyatira, Sardis, and Laodicea, there is that in Philadelphia that appeals to the heart of Christ, for Philadelphia is a state of reality in persons that gives Him great pleasure. He speaks about persons “who say that they are Jews, and are not, but lie” (Revelation 3: 9), that is, persons who profess to be the real thing but are not. O, dear brethren, let us be wholly free from that! Feeding on the passover Lamb and the unleavened bread will keep us free of hypocrisy, lying, and all that kind of thing, and bring about in us a state of sincerity and truth, of reality and transparency, that is so delightful to the heart of Christ. In Revelation 11 John is told to measure the temple of God, and the altar, and them that worship in it, but not to measure the court for it represents mere profession, an unreal state of things displeasing to Christ. But the temple (the shrine itself), the altar, and the worshippers are measured because they represent conditions of reality secured spiritually by God in faithful persons at a time when evil is reaching a climax in Jerusalem.

Well, Azariah is a man who has come under the measuring reed and the Spirit’s assessment is, “He is it”. My earnest desire is that He may be able to say of each one present, ‘He (or she) is it’. This man was a prince. He was one of Solomon’s princes (see 1 Kings 4: 2). Indeed, all the men in high office in Solomon’s regime were princes, that is, they were men of moral worth and spiritual stature, personalities formed by the Spirit. The office did not make these men for, morally and spiritually, they were at least equal to, if not greater than, the office they filled, hence the effectiveness of their administration. In the world princes are born and a man carries the title ‘prince’ no matter how weak he may be morally, even though he be a good-for-nothing. God makes His princes (see Psalm 45: 16). The history of Jacob in Genesis shows us the making of a prince. This involves much secret history with God, going over matters in deep soul exercise alone with Him. Then He disciplines us in various ways as part of the making process.

Thank God, He is over the refining process Himself for He knows the end He wants to reach in us (see Malachi 3: 3). Israel was “formed”, Isaiah 43: 1. What a prince Jacob was when he went in to the presence of the greatest earthly potentate of the day and blessed Pharaoh! Beyond all gainsaying, the inferior was blessed by the better. Israel, the prince of God, outshone Pharaoh morally. So, dear brethren, let us not seek after earthly glory for it is passing and will come to nothing, but rather let us submit ourselves to the will of God in His dealings with us in view of making us princes for His realm. In Numbers 7, at the dedication of the altar, we see the greatness of God’s princes and the wealth of their offerings. What is stressed is the weight of the vessels and the quality of the substance in them, which shows that these were men of moral weight, full of spiritual substance, and their offering gave God so much pleasure that, as we have been taught. He caused them to be spread over twelve days, giving each prince a day to himself, and then He takes account of the aggregate. Well, dear brethren, as we go over these things it is to encourage us to be like this man Azariah, princely, the real thing.

Then it says he “exercised the priesthood”. Notice it does not say, ‘He was priest’. The writer of Chronicles views things from the standpoint of the breakdown and the recovery, hence he does not call attention to what is official but rather to moral qualities in persons, so that he speaks about the man and what he is doing. These are days for doing things, as Paul says to Timothy, “Do the work of an evangelist”, 2 Timothy 4: 5. This is the same principle here; the man is doing the work, exercising the priesthood. He is not only taking up the privilege but accepting fully the responsibility of furnishing what would minister to God’s pleasure, and also maintaining all that is due to God in His dwelling-place. O, dear brethren, that is the greatest service that has been entrusted to us—to provide in a priestly way what is for the pleasure of God and to maintain holy conditions in His sanctuary. Let us then keep by the Holy Spirit what has been committed to us. Things in christendom are at a very low ebb generally but let us not lower the standard in any way.

The state of things in the priesthood was very low in the opening chapters of 1 Samuel. Eli, the official priest, was lethargic and apathetic, and his sons had made themselves vile, yet in the midst of such conditions a man of God reminds Eli of the true function of the priesthood (see 1 Samuel 2: 27, 28). First of all he reminds him of God’s sovereignty, that He chose Levi out of all the tribes of Israel to be His priest. The fact that God sovereignly selected us to serve Him as priests should make a powerful appeal to all our hearts. Why did God choose me and not someone else? Why did He take me up on the ground of redemption? Surely it was to consider for Him and for His pleasure, “to offer upon mine altar”. When we read through the offerings we are impressed with the great amount and the large variety—daily offerings, offerings on the sabbath, offerings on the set feasts, besides the voluntary offerings. It was the priests’ responsibility to offer the continual offerings. So today, beloved, it is our responsibility to offer to God what gives Him pleasure. What a responsibility—but what a privilege!—to provide sacrificially what means so much to the heart of God, “to burn incense”. This was to be done every day and it involved the priest going in to the altar of incense in the holy place.

One thought in regard of incense is that it is the prayers of the saints (see Revelation 5: 8). It is right to pray for our own needs, but burning incense is rather giving ourselves to praying for divine interests, to praying for the saints in relation to God’s thoughts for them. The prayers of Paul in Ephesians 1 and 3, and in Philippians 1, are examples of this. We might think ‘That is Paul’, but the Spirit calls attention to the prayers of Epaphras in Colossians 4: 12. There is a local brother functioning as a priest at the golden altar, and his prayers are fragrant to God. The Spirit would help us to maintain our prayers at this level, as Paul says, “prayer and supplication in the Spirit”, Ephesians 6: 18.

Then the word to Eli was that the priest was “To wear the ephod before me”. The ephod is the priestly garment, and God looks for those who draw near to Him to be characterized by features that are suited to His presence. Those who serve God must be characterized by practical righteousness and holiness. Then, to comment further on that section in 1 Samuel 2, we read, “I gave unto the house of thy father all the offerings by fire of the children of Israel”. Think of that—the food that God Himself feeds upon, reverently speaking, becomes the food of the priests. We have had before us today the passover, the unleavened bread, and the bread in the Supper as food, but what food this is, as Mr. Darby says,
‘His Father Thou, and ours through grace,
We taste the same delight’. (Hymn 26)
It is wonderful that God shares with His priests the delight that He finds in Christ, for all the offerings speak of Christ, and as we feed on Christ it brings about in us correspondence to Him.

Well, Azariah was the real thing and he exercised the priesthood in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem. Solomon is a type of Christ in glory and the house he built is a type of the assembly in its heavenly relations with Christ. We might speak of it as Paul’s assembly, the assembly as presented to us in Ephesians. Corinthians is the assembly in the wilderness, the abode of God’s holiness. The tabernacle in the wilderness was anointed, having in mind power and dignity in the testimonial position, but this house was not anointed, for it represents the assembly in its intrinsic worth. The Lord’s references to the “treasure” and the “pearl” in Matthew 13, and Paul’s words “the assembly of God, which he has purchased with the blood of his own” (Acts 20: 28), bring before us the assembly in its intrinsic worth.

Do we really value the grace that has given us a part and place in such a glorious vessel, where God is served, where there is glory to God? Do we really value the great ministry of the first half of this century which bore so much upon Christ and the assembly and the service of God? David said that the house must be exceeding great in fame and in beauty (see 1 Chronicles 22: 5). What tremendous wealth he provided so unselfishly for it, in his affection, in his affliction, and according to all his power. Solomon said that the house was to be “great and wonderful”, 2 Chronicles 2: 9. The assembly, this glorious heavenly vessel, is great and wonderful. It is so because it is the vessel of God’s purpose, because of what Christ gave for it—He gave Himself—and because of the vast expenditure of the Holy Spirit in relation to it in His unremitting service of tireless love all these years since Pentecost. Well, beloved brethren, it is ours now to minister to the pleasure of God in such a vessel, and to maintain fully and faithfully all that is due to Him in it as real persons. May it be so, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: SPIRITUAL PERSONALITY
articles.author: M. B. Thompson
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn., N.Y.

paragraphs.text: I was thinking about the idea of spiritual personality. It is interesting that the dispensation began with personality. Acts 1 gives a list of names and then speaks of “the crowd of names”, as though the Spirit is drawing our attention to spiritual personality. It is superfluous to say that it has been seen in this city. You come here and you think about the long history of spiritual personality that has been here. One rejoices in it! It is a thing that we should look for at the close of the dispensation.. I think the dispensation will close the way it began, and I would like to look to my local meeting and to myself, for instance, to see that the features that were seen when the christian dispensation was inaugurated are there at the end. You would not like things to go out in decline, would you? We would not like our local meetings to go out in decline. I think the way things will be maintained will be by spiritual personality among the saints, personality that can be identified.

Here in Judges is a woman who says, “Until that I Deborah arose, That I arose a mother in Israel”. You might say that was her identity, a mother in Israel. That is a very needed feature; you can see the need for spiritual personality in the feature of the mother. How much that is needed in local meetings, that there are those in whom is the identifiable feature of a mother in Israel. I think it is very remarkable that here is somebody who is doing things because there is a need of things being done. She says, “I Deborah arose, That I arose a mother in Israel”; she obviously had some concern about the situation, and she arose and did what was needed. I think that feature needs to be cultivated and nurtured in our local meetings, the feature of the mother. Mr. Taylor pointed out, regarding the work of God in those that come in in the Revelation, that they can be identified (N.S. Vol. 48 p.124). He takes up the idea of the one hundred and forty four thousand and says there are features about them that can be identified. Well, can I identify myself with those features? It says of that company that they follow the Lamb wheresoever it goes (see Revelation 14: 4). Is that characteristic seen with us? It is personality, so that the work of God can be identified in us. I think that is the way things will be maintained. I think this scripture proves that that is the way the position was saved; somebody had a concern and did the needed service. Does it not say that about Phoebe that she did the needed service?—there was something to be done and she did it (see Romans 16: 1, footnote).

Paul shines out in a distinctive way wherever you see him. Is that not fine? He is able to say, “I myself, Paul, entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of the Christ”. He is able to identify these features in himself. He must have been a very personable, a very presentable, man. It says of David that he was of beautiful appearance (1 Samuel 16: 12); he must have had great personality. Think of how they came to him; they felt safe with David as they came to him in the cave of Adullam—persons who were in debt, of embittered spirit, yet they all came to David. He must have been a very personable man that they came to him and put their trust in him. Paul would be like that; you could trust him. He says when speaking to these beloved saints, “I entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of the Christ”. He says, ‘I am speaking to you myself’, and yet in the way he does it there are identifiable features of Christ, “the meekness and gentleness of the Christ”. Chapter 10 and onwards has been called the militant ministry of Paul, and yet he says, the way I am going about it is with the meekness and gentleness of the Christ. I think that is very wonderful, the features of Christ coming out in somebody, and that is their personality. He says, “I myself, Paul”; is that not fine? Would you not listen to his words if he had written to you? Philemon received that letter in which Paul uses such skill. He says to Philemon, ‘Just take it from me; I am an old man’—“Being such a one as Paul the aged” (Philemon 9). You could hardly think of Philemon doing anything else than accepting Paul’s admonition.

I thought of John because he is a follower of Christ. Would you not like that to be a characteristic of your personality, that you are a follower of Christ? Peter saw the one whom Jesus loved following and he says, “What of this man?”, John 21: 21. John just seems to be a characteristic follower of Christ. That enters into his personality. Here he says, “I John, your brother and fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience in Jesus”. He says, I am just your brother. You will have noticed that the Lord does not give him any commission at all in John 21. He says to Peter, “Feed my lambs”, “Shepherd my sheep”, “Feed my sheep”, but He does not say anything to John. John says, ‘I am just your brother’. Is it not a fine thing to have a brother like that in your local meeting? Are you not thankful many a time for a brother in your local meeting, a brother and fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience in Jesus? He says, I am not with you in body, yet I am “your brother and fellow-partaker”. If that was moulded into your personality, that you were just a brother, what a fine thing that would be! There it is, that you have a brother in your local meeting, somebody who, whatever you are going through, enters into it with you. We had a touch recently about the difference between sympathy and comfort; you might express your sympathy to somebody, but for somebody to come along and give comfort—that is the feature of the brother. Whatever the saints are going through he is alongside of them, and the saints are going through some very grievous things. We have had some very grievous exercises on our side, very serious illnesses, sudden deaths, and things like that; well, you need the brother, somebody that is partaking in the same things. We hear of the sorrows that have come in in New Zealand through departure, deep family sorrow; you might say that what is needed is the brother, somebody that realises what the saints are going through, “your brother and fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience, in Jesus”.

Paul says, “Sosthenes the brother”, 1 Corinthians 1: 2. Is that not a fine thing? I feel the need of these features; and in some sense as you see a lack you would like to fill it out. After all, spiritual personality is developed on that line. It is what you get from Christ.

There has been a tremendous amount of sorrow, and what the brethren need is encouragement. Think of the disciples after having gone through the sorrow of the exercises when the Lord was taken from them, and then to be all together in the upper room. The Spirit seems to delight in bringing, forward the spiritual personalities; one hundred and fifty three great fish were in that net in John 21. I think it shows that there must have been spiritual quality and personality, and that comes out in the book of the Acts. I think the Lord looks, and He is entitled to look, for something of the same character in the last days. May we be encouraged on that line for His name’s sake.
Thy life Thou didst lay down, O Lord,
Such was Thy Father’s will;
His rights to Him Thou would’st accord,
His pleasure all fulfil.
Although this act was all Thine own
(None took Thy life from Thee),
Thou waited’st for His time alone,
And His authority.
On this account Thy Father’s love,
Not new, but freshly moved,
Shone down on Thee from heav’n above;
Obedience fully proved!
For us, Thy sheep, Thou did’st lay down
That life—good Shepherd Thou,
To form one flock of all Thine own,
Responsive to Thee now.
The bands of death have all been freed,
Death had o’er Thee no right—
The life laid down Thou hast anew
In resurrection’s might.

The Lord ... would bring about the spirit of search, for a great many of our brethren are lost to us, and if we are near the Father and the Son and the Spirit, we shall be made conscious of that. They are lost, and you are not at rest till they are all found. The man that failed as king is the man who did not find the asses. You may be greater than other brethren, but the test of your efficiency is that you find those that are lost. May the Lord give us to seek our brethren!
A man of God is morally the greatest title you can get; a man of God is a man who is with God, and has partaken of His character.
